blocks.text: A billboard along the Lagos–Ibadan expressway is held up by two steel cables pulling at an angle and by its own weight pulling down. It does not move, so those three forces must cancel exactly. Working out what each cable carries is a problem in the equilibrium of forces — and the same method holds a bridge up.

blocks.markdown:
A force is a vector, so two forces do not simply add as numbers. To combine them you use the **parallelogram law**: draw the two forces from the same point as adjacent sides of a parallelogram, and the diagonal from that point gives the **resultant**.

For two forces at right angles this reduces to Pythagoras:

$$R = \sqrt{F_1^{2} + F_2^{2}}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{F_2}{F_1}$$

blocks.title: Resultant and equilibrant
blocks.text: The resultant is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together. The equilibrant is the single force that would hold the system in equilibrium — equal in magnitude to the resultant but opposite in direction.

blocks.caption: General resultant of two forces with angle θ between them; θ = 90° reduces this to Pythagoras

blocks.title: Resultant of two perpendicular forces
blocks.prompt: Forces of 3.0 N and 4.0 N act at right angles to each other at a point. Find the magnitude and direction of their resultant.

steps.text: Because the forces are perpendicular, use Pythagoras' theorem for the magnitude.
Evaluate the square root, keeping the unit.
For the direction, take the angle measured from the 3.0 N force.

blocks.answer: R = 5.0 N at 53.1° to the 3.0 N force

blocks.markdown:
### Resolving a force

The reverse process is just as useful. Any single force $F$ acting at angle $\theta$ to a chosen direction can be replaced by two perpendicular components:

$$F_x = F\cos\theta, \qquad F_y = F\sin\theta$$

The cosine always goes with the direction the angle is measured **from**. Resolving turns an awkward two-dimensional problem into two independent one-dimensional problems.

blocks.title: A block on a smooth inclined plane
blocks.prompt: A block of weight 200 N rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Find the component of its weight (a) along the plane and (b) perpendicular to the plane.

steps.text: The weight acts vertically downwards. Resolve it into a component down the slope and one pressing into the slope. For a slope of angle θ, the component along the plane uses sin θ.
The component perpendicular to the plane uses cos θ.
Check: the perpendicular component equals the normal reaction on a smooth plane, and the two components combine back to 200 N since √(100² + 173²) ≈ 200.

blocks.answer: (a) 100 N down the plane  (b) 173 N perpendicular to the plane

blocks.markdown:
### Conditions for equilibrium

A rigid body is in equilibrium when **both** of these hold:

1. The vector sum of all the forces is zero — equivalently, $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$. This prevents linear acceleration.
2. The algebraic sum of the moments about **any** point is zero. This prevents rotation.

A body can satisfy the first and still fail the second: two equal, opposite forces along different lines form a **couple**, which does not move the body along but spins it.

rows: Equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, along the same line
Their vector diagram forms a closed triangle (triangle of forces)
Lami's theorem: F₁/sin α = F₂/sin β = F₃/sin γ
Closed polygon of forces, and zero total moment

blocks.title: Maximum and minimum resultant
blocks.text: Two forces give their largest resultant when they act in the same direction (F₁ + F₂) and their smallest when they oppose each other (|F₁ − F₂|). Any resultant between those two limits is possible for some angle. Questions often ask for exactly these bounds.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Recognise the 3–4–5 and 5–12–13 right-angled triangles instantly. Forces of 3 N and 4 N perpendicular give 5 N; 5 N and 12 N give 13 N; 6 N and 8 N give 10 N. Examiners choose these numbers deliberately, and spotting them saves you a full minute per question.

points: Forces are vectors, so combine them using the parallelogram law, not simple addition.
For perpendicular forces, R = √(F₁² + F₂²) and tan θ = F₂ ÷ F₁.
Resolving a force F at angle θ gives components F cos θ and F sin θ along perpendicular directions.
The equilibrant is equal and opposite to the resultant.
Equilibrium needs both zero resultant force and zero total moment about any point.
